A Grammar of Machine Learning Workflows

Simon Roth
2026-03-01
Abstract

Data leakage affected 294 published papers across 17 scientific fields ([ref-kapoor2023leakage]). The dominant response has been documentation: checklists, linters, best-practice guides. Documentation does not prevent these failures. A structural remedy exists: a grammar that decomposes the supervised learning lifecycle into 7 kernel primitives connected by a typed directed acyclic graph (DAG), with four hard constraints that reject the two most damaging leakage classes at call time. Invalid compositions within the grammar’s seven primitives are rejected by type checks or call-time guards. For compliant usage, detection becomes unnecessary. The grammar’s core contribution is the terminal assess constraint: a runtime-enforced evaluate/assess boundary where repeated test-set assessment is rejected by a guard on a nominally distinct Evidence type, making test-set reuse rejected at call time within the grammar’s API. My companion study across 2,047 experimental instances ([ref-roth2026landscape], in preparation) quantifies why this matters: selection leakage inflates performance by dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93 (raw AUC inflation: +0.046+0.046 points, 95% CI [0.043,0.048][0.043,0.048]) and memorization leakage by dz=0.53d_{z}=0.53–1.111.11, scaling with model capacity, while estimation leakage is negligible (|d|<0.1|d|<0.1). A follow-up study across 3,759 additional instances establishes that Class II effects persist at all tested sample sizes: a power law fit produces a positive asymptotic floor of d∞=0.047d_{\infty}=0.047 (N=493N=493 datasets), confirming that the grammar’s unconditional rejection is empirically necessary within the tested range (n=50n=50–2,0002{,}000). The grammar generated three falsifiable predictions before observing experimental results. Two confirmed, one falsified. The grammar survives empirical test. Three separate implementations (Python, R, and Julia) confirm the claims. The appendix specification lets anyone build a conforming version.

1 Introduction

Kapoor and Narayanan ([ref-kapoor2023leakage]) audited the machine learning literature and found data leakage errors in 294 published papers across 17 scientific fields. This is not a knowledge gap: Kaufman et al. ([ref-kaufman2012leakage]) formalized the leakage taxonomy a decade earlier. Cawley and Talbot ([ref-cawley2010overfitting]) demonstrated selection bias in model evaluation fifteen years ago. The problem persists because documentation does not prevent these failures. It affects 17.5% of neuroimaging studies ([ref-rosenblatt2024data]) and propagates into field-level meta-analytic conclusions ([ref-vandemortel2025leakage]).

The response to this crisis has been documentation: best-practice guides, checklists, linting tools. Yang, Breck, and Whang ([ref-yang2022leakage]) built LeakageDetector, achieving 92.9% accuracy on three leakage types, demonstrating that detection is feasible. A natural follow-up question is whether prevention is also possible: can leakage be made to fail at call time by the composition rules of the workflow itself, rather than detected after the fact? This paper addresses that question for tabular supervised learning — binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression — on the three leakage classes for which effect sizes have been empirically quantified. Temporal leakage, target leakage, and distribution mismatch are real problems the grammar does not currently address; extending the type DAG to cover them requires empirical baselines analogous to those established for Classes I–III.

The history of formal grammars suggests it can. In every domain where practitioners composed complex artifacts from simpler parts, a grammar eventually emerged that separated valid from invalid compositions:

All five entries share a common move: enumerating the primitives of a domain. But they differ on composition. Bertin catalogued visual channels by perceptual capacity: a taxonomy that identified primitives without defining rules for combining them or criteria for rejecting invalid combinations. Chomsky, Codd, Wilkinson, and Wickham went further: each defined composition rules and a rejection criterion that makes “this is wrong” a formal statement rather than an opinion. “Grammar” here follows Chomsky rather than Wilkinson: a finite rule system that partitions sequences into well-formed and ill-formed, not a combinatorial algebra of independently composable layers. The grammars that survived had executable implementations: SQL for Codd, ggplot2 for Wickham, parsers for Chomsky. Without one, a grammar stays academic.

The Wickham gap. Wickham ([ref-wickham2010layered])’s contribution was not the API; it was the successful implementation and selection. ggplot2 is not a complete implementation of Wilkinson’s full system; it exposes a curated subset of it. By choosing which primitives to make primary and which to omit, Wickham shifted which errors were easy to make: incomplete specifications fail at construction, and correct compositions become the default path. The analogous selection has not been made for the ML lifecycle. Kuhn and Silge ([ref-kuhn2022tidy]) made the most important prior contribution: recipes inside workflows enforce per-fold preprocessing, structurally preventing Class I leakage. The remaining question is whether the type system can go one level further — distinguishing “this data has been split correctly” from “this data has not,” and marking a model as terminally assessed. tidymodels types serve implementation correctness (recipe, parsnip model, workflow); the grammar adds a methodological correctness layer on top (Partition, PreparedData, Model with assessed state).

This paper makes that selection for supervised learning.

2 A Motivating Example

Consider a binary classification task. The standard workflow in scikit-learn ([ref-pedregosa2011sklearn]):

# Standard sklearn — Pipeline fixes this; the grammar goes further

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

scaler = StandardScaler()

X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X) # Leaks: sees test rows

scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_scaled, y, cv=5)

print(f"CV AUC: {scores.mean():.3f}") # Optimistic

The scaler sees all rows before the cross-validation split. This is Class I leakage (estimation bias). Its effect is negligible (d≈0d\approx 0; Roth ([ref-roth2026landscape])). The canonical sklearn fix (wrapping scaler and classifier in a Pipeline) solves this case cleanly by keeping preprocessing inside the cross-validation loop. The grammar builds on that insight and extends it to the next boundary: distinguishing evaluation from assessment, enforcing assess-once, and addressing the more damaging Class II (dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93) and Class III (dz=0.53d_{z}=0.53–1.111.11) patterns that operate above the preprocessing level. The normalization example is used here because it is structurally visible; the grammar’s contribution starts where Pipeline’s protection ends.

The grammar version:

import ml

s = ml.split(df, target="y", seed=42)

model = ml.fit(s.train, "y", algorithm="rf", seed=42)

metrics = ml.evaluate(model, s.valid)

final = ml.assess(model, test=s.test)

Each line produces a typed output that constrains what the next line can accept. fit requires a Partition’s training fold, not raw data. assess requires a Model that has not been previously assessed. Preparation happens inside fit, per fold, by default. The leaky workflow is rejected: scaler.fit_transform(X) on the full dataset produces a DataFrame that was never registered by split. When that result is passed to fit, the provenance guard rejects it: the data has no split provenance. The grammar rejects it at call time, not after the fact.

3 The Grammar

3.1 Kernel primitives

The grammar decomposes 36 API verbs into 7 kernel primitives:

assess returns Evidence: a nominally distinct type with no downstream consumers. No primitive accepts Evidence as input. It flows to the human, not to the next step. explain is similarly terminal: its output feeds no further primitive.

explain is the grammar’s unconstrained primitive. Every other kernel primitive carries at least one partition guard: split accepts any DataFrame; prepare and fit require registered {train, valid, dev}-tagged data; evaluate rejects test-tagged and unregistered data. assess requires test-tagged data and fires once per model. explain requires only a fitted Model. It may be called on any data, any number of times, before or after assess. Explanation is diagnostic, not part of the validity chain. explain is outside the grammar’s rejection criterion by design: the grammar has no partition guard to place on it.

The assess-once constraint is enforced by the call-time guard model.assessed = false, which fires before the call completes. A second call assess(model, test=s.test) still passes the type check (the model argument is still a Model) but fails the guard, which then raises. This is a guard rejection, not a type error. It requires runtime state and cannot be caught by a type-checker before the call executes. This distinction is discussed in Section 4.

Declarative default: fit accepts a tagged DataFrame (partition_tag in {train, valid}) and handles preparation internally, per fold. In explicit mode, the user calls ml.prepare() first, receiving a PreparedData object; fit then accepts PreparedData as input instead. Both modes satisfy the same guards. The correct workflow should be the obvious choice; calling prepare explicitly is available but never required.

Why fit accepts valid-tagged data. The {train, valid} guard allows refitting on combined train+validation data after hyperparameter selection is complete, before the final terminal assessment. This is the dev = train + valid workflow. It is not a guard relaxation; it is a recognized final-preparation step before assess.

The iterative/final fit distinction. The type signature fit :: DataFrame × target → Model is identical whether fit is called during the iterate zone (training a candidate model per fold, evaluated and discarded) or as the final fit(dev) call after hyperparameters are fixed. These two roles differ in commitment: per-fold models are expendable. The final fit(dev) model is the one that proceeds to assess. The grammar assigns both calls the same type because they satisfy the same preconditions. The semantic distinction (which fit is final) is invisible to the type system. A practitioner who treats a per-fold model as the committed model makes a semantic error, not a structural one. The diagnostics layer (check, report) catches it. The type DAG does not.

Primitive count. Seven is empirical, not derived — the smallest set of operations practitioners actually perform that covers them without collapsing a type boundary or losing a postcondition. The clearest case: predict and evaluate both consume a Model, but they carry different guards. predict imposes no partition constraint (it is valid on any data, including untagged deployment data), while evaluate requires partition_tag = valid. Merging them forces a choice: adopt the stricter guard and break the deploy use case, or adopt the weaker guard and allow evaluation on untagged or training data. Either way, a guard that exists only because the primitives are separate collapses. The same argument applies to each: split alone produces a Partition. prepare alone fits and returns a reusable Transformer state (absorbing it into fit destroys the ability to apply consistent preprocessing to held-out data without refitting). assess alone produces Evidence. Removing any one loses either a type or a guard that the rejection criterion depends on.

3.2 The type DAG

The primitives connect through a typed directed acyclic graph (Figure 1). Reading top to bottom: a single DataFrame enters a split decision (diamond), which routes data into three named partitions — train, valid, and test. The train and valid partitions feed a fit/evaluate loop (the cycle on the left of the diagram) where the practitioner iterates freely: fitting models, inspecting validation metrics, adjusting hyperparameters. The test partition, by contrast, is gated (marked ×\times): it remains locked until the practitioner calls assess exactly once, producing terminal evidence that the grammar does not allow to be revisited. The visual asymmetry is the point; iteration is cheap and encouraged, commitment is expensive and irreversible.

The Partition type has two variants:

The split primitive accepts awareness parameters that compose with both variants: stratify=True (class balance, default), groups="patient_id" (group membership), time="date" (temporal order). Every awareness parameter addresses a specific leakage mechanism.

split is the most parameterized primitive. split(groups="patient_id") and split(time="date") produce Partitions with qualitatively different validity properties: GroupKFold forbids group overlap across folds. PurgedKFold additionally enforces temporal ordering and an embargo gap. These are not separate primitives — they are domain specializations of one primitive. All variants share the type signature DataFrame → Partition. What differs is the guard system. split_temporal carries guards that split does not: embargo enforcement, expanding-vs-sliding window policy, temporal ordering with no future leakage. split_group carries a group-non-overlap guard that is meaningless for random splits. The specializations are constraint profiles, not type distinctions: each conjugates the same grammatical verb for a different scientific domain (time series forecasting, clinical trials with repeated measures, standard cross-sectional ML). The primitive count remains 7. The implementation exposes split, split_temporal, and split_group as independent entry points, each with domain-specific parameters and error messages, rather than burying the domain logic behind parameter combinations on a single function. This is a design choice: the grammar’s type system sees one primitive; the API surface reflects that different fields require different structural constraints on the same partitioning operation.

3.3 The four hard constraints

The constraints are empirically grounded. In the companion study ([ref-roth2026landscape]), Class II effects (dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93, raw AUC inflation +0.046+0.046) and Class III effects (dz=0.53d_{z}=0.53–1.111.11) are large enough to invalidate published results. A follow-up study across 493 datasets at six sample sizes (3,759 experimental instances total) confirms that Class II effects persist with a positive asymptotic floor (d∞=0.047d_{\infty}=0.047), establishing that the grammar’s rejection is empirically necessary within the tested range. Class I effects are negligible (d≈0d\approx 0), but Constraint 2 is retained because it is principled (consistent with all textbook recommendations) and costless (per-fold preparation is the default).

The constraints are also minimal: 4 rules, not 40. Chomsky’s programme stalled when syntactic rules proliferated to cover semantic territory. Codd’s relational model succeeded by stating a small number of inviolable properties and leaving optimization to implementations. More rules do not necessarily mean better protection.

3.4 Strategy families

The 7 primitives compose into 4 strategy families covering the full developmental workflow:

The strategies decompose into kernel primitives:

  • •

    screen: ∀\forall algo: fit →\to evaluate →\to rank →\to Leaderboard

  • •

    tune: ∀\forall params: fit →\to evaluate →\to select_best →\to TuningResult

  • •

    stack: ∀\forall model: fit →\to out-of-fold predict →\to fit_meta →\to StackedModel

No strategy requires a new primitive: each reduces to typed applications of the 7 kernel verbs. That the core developmental workflow fits within this decomposition (for the strategies examined here) is evidence that the primitives capture structure, not an accidental API boundary. The output containers Leaderboard, TuningResult, and StackedModel are informal wrappers for composition results; they are convenience wrappers, not part of the workflow grammar itself.

The erased intermediate in tune. The tune decomposition hides a type the grammar does not declare: after select_best identifies optimal parameters, those parameters — a HyperParameters intermediate — feed the final fit(dev) call. The grammar’s visible type chain is TuningResult → fit → Model; the HyperParameters intermediate exists in every implementation but is not a sort in the type DAG. This is a deliberate compression: tune is a strategy, not a primitive, and its internal types are outside the grammar’s minimal vocabulary. A conforming extension could expose HyperParameters as a declared sort with its own typed accessor from TuningResult, making the refitting step explicit and enabling a guard that rejects fit(dev) called without a completed tune cycle.

Grammar predictions. The constraints and composition rules generate testable predictions: if a strategy violates a constraint, measurable inflation should follow. Three were tested in the companion study before observing V2 results:

Two of three confirmed. One falsified. The falsified prediction is evidence that the grammar generates specific, wrong-able hypotheses, not post-hoc rationalization. The full experimental results are in Section 7.3.

3.5 The terminal boundary

The evaluate/assess distinction is the grammar’s central structural claim.

  • •

    Evaluate operates on validation data. It is repeatable, cheap, and safe for decisions. It informs the iterate cycle: the practitioner reads the Metrics output, adjusts, and fits again. Metrics is terminal in the type system (no primitive accepts it as input), but it drives iteration at the practitioner level.

  • •

    Assess operates on test data. It is terminal, once per model, and irreversible. It is a deliberate commit: the model’s performance on data it has never influenced.

The distinction encodes the textbook structure of model assessment ([ref-hastie2009elements]). Generalization error (§7.1) becomes assess producing Evidence: frozen, terminal, unrevisitable. Training error is available internally but not reported. Model assessment (§7.2) is evaluate on validation, repeatable by design. Model selection maps to the Selection and Optimization families. Cross-validation (§7.10) is split(folds=k) feeding the Evaluation family. The two textbook failure modes (preprocessing before splitting at §7.10.2, “the wrong way”; reusing the test set at §7.7) map directly to Constraints 4, 2, and 1. A student who learns ML with this grammar internalizes the separation from day one. The evaluate/assess distinction, explained in every textbook and violated in 294 papers, is enforced by the types, not by the student’s memory.

4 Design Properties

The three properties below are design constraints, not theorems. Codd’s data independence and Wickham’s layer independence play the same role in their grammars. Any proposed extension can be validated against them. So can any third-party implementation.

The word “grammar” here follows Wilkinson and Wickham, not Chomsky. A Chomsky grammar generates strings by derivation rules; this grammar generates typed workflows enforced by the type DAG and call-time guards. The two senses are not equivalent, but the term is retained because it is the established name in the Wilkinson–Wickham tradition that this work extends.

The grammar uses two kinds of rejection. Structural rejection (type mismatch) is static: a function that accepts Model cannot receive a Partition. Guard rejection is dynamic: it requires runtime state (e.g., model.assessed = false) and fires before the call completes. The four hard constraints use both mechanisms: assess-once is a guard; the type DAG prevents nonsensical type chains structurally. The workflow’s valid state transitions form a regular language recognizable by a 4-state deterministic finite automaton (DFA) with states {CREATED,FITTED,EVALUATED,ASSESSED}\{\text{CREATED},\text{FITTED},\text{EVALUATED},\text{ASSESSED}\}. ASSESSED is a terminal sink that rejects all further transitions. The primary path is FITTED→EVALUATED→ASSESSED\text{FITTED}\to\text{EVALUATED}\to\text{ASSESSED}, but a shortcut FITTED→ASSESSED\text{FITTED}\to\text{ASSESSED} is valid (assessing without prior evaluation). Repeatable verbs (explain, predict, calibrate, validate) are self-loops that preserve the current state. The Python implementation tracks this DFA on every Model object; the state machine is the algebraic backbone of the guard system.

4.1 Reachability

Every type in the DAG is reachable from DataFrame through the primitives. The non-terminal types (DataFrame, Partition, PreparedData, Model) form a chain: each is produced by one primitive and consumed by the next. The terminal types (Predictions, Metrics, Evidence, Explanation) are all reachable from Model. No type is orphaned. Any conforming extension must preserve this connectivity. The property is reachability (every type can be reached from the root), not closure in Codd’s sense.

In the relational algebra, every operator returns a relation, so operators compose freely (Codd-closure: op​(R)→R\text{op}(R)\to R). The grammar has no such property: predict returns Predictions, not a DataFrame, so split cannot follow predict. This is deliberate. Codd maximized composability; the grammar maximizes structural safety. A fully closed ML grammar would allow leaky workflows; the type restrictions that prevent leakage are exactly the restrictions that break free composability. The tradeoff is intentional.

4.2 Generativity

The set of valid workflows the grammar can express is infinite: because the fit/evaluate loop can repeat any number of times, split → (fit → evaluate)n → assess is valid for any nn. Each fit and evaluate call draws from the same Partition produced by split, not from the Metrics output of the previous evaluate (which is terminal). The cycle exists in the workflow pattern, not in the linear type chain. The grammar does not cap iteration depth.

Scope. The grammar covers batch supervised learning on a complete dataset available at split time. Multi-task learning (multiple simultaneous targets), self-supervised learning (no explicit labels), few-shot learning (NN too small to partition meaningfully), federated learning (data never centralized), and online learning (incremental data arrival) each violate at least one foundational assumption and fall outside the grammar’s scope. The grammar generates all valid workflows within its scope. It makes no claim about valid ML workflows in general.

4.3 Rejection criterion

The grammar makes specific workflows invalid. Each is rejected by a type check or a call-time guard:

Assess-once (by construction). Constraint 1 specifies: for Model mm, assess(mm, test) is valid if and only if mm.assessed = false. After the first call, mm.assessed ←\leftarrow true. The second call fails the guard. Similarly, prepare(all_data) before split violates Constraint 2 (the data is unregistered in the provenance registry, so the guard rejects it), and select_features(X, y) before split violates Constraint 4. All three are rejected at call time. These are not theorems; they are consequences of the type guards. The claim is that any conforming implementation must enforce them. The Appendix (§ Invalid workflows as guard failures) walks through each entry in the table above.

This grammar is a rejection function: its value lies not in the workflows it enables but in the workflows it makes impossible to execute within its API boundary.

The rejection here is positional, not structural. Chomsky’s grammar makes certain strings underivable: the invalid form cannot be generated at all. Codd’s constraints make certain states unstorable: the invalid row cannot exist in the relation. The ML grammar is weaker on both counts: fit(test_data, target) is a valid Python expression, a valid R call, a valid Julia invocation. The invalid workflow is representable in the host language. What the grammar rejects is the transition: test-tagged data entering fit is immediately blocked by a guard that checks a content-addressed partition registry external to the DataFrame. The guard rejects the call, not the code. fit(test_data) is valid Python, but the registry lookup makes it fail at call time. This is a necessary consequence of embedding a grammar in a host language that has no native partition type. The grammar operates at verb entry points, not at the level of the host language’s type system.

All four constraints are purely negative: they define the boundary of valid workflows without ranking or recommending within it. The grammar does not specify which algorithm to choose, how many folds to use, or when to stop iterating; those are semantics-layer decisions. This is the Codd pattern. The relational model rejects invalid queries without suggesting good ones. The positive structure of a good ML workflow is the diagnostics and strategy layer’s job, not the grammar’s.

The property that certain leakage-producing workflows are rejected at call time — by guard failure or type mismatch, not detected after the fact — is, to my knowledge, not present in any existing ML framework as a terminal assess-once constraint. The grammar does not lint completed workflows. It rejects invalid ones as they are constructed. This claim is bounded to the grammar’s own type system: operations outside the grammar’s seven primitives can always produce leakage that the grammar cannot see.

The workflow’s structural guarantees are a minimum over its constituent primitives: a violation at split() propagates through all downstream operations, and no downstream primitive recovers correctness from an upstream violation. This is why the four hard constraints are placed at split and prepare rather than at assess: the terminal boundary is too late to undo upstream contamination.

5 Embedding in Code

5.1 Triple implementation

The grammar is implemented in three languages: Python (mlw on PyPI, imported as import ml; source: github.com/epagogy/ml), R (ml, CRAN submission in progress), and Julia (ML.jl). All three expose the same 7 kernel primitives with identical type signatures:

# Python

import ml

s = ml.split(df, target="y", seed=42)

model = ml.fit(s.train, "y", algorithm="rf", seed=42)

metrics = ml.evaluate(model, s.valid)

final = ml.assess(model, test=s.test)

# R

library(ml)

s <- ml_split(df, target="y", seed=42)

model <- ml_fit(s$train, "y", algorithm="rf", seed=42)

metrics <- ml_evaluate(model, s$valid)

final <- ml_assess(model, test=s$test)

# Julia

using ML

s = ML.split(df, "y"; seed=42)

model = ML.fit(s.train, "y"; algorithm="rf", seed=42)

metrics = ML.evaluate(model, s.valid)

final = ML.assess(model; test=s.test)

The Julia implementation is the grammar’s independent portability test. It was built from the appendix specification without translating Python or R code, using Julia-native libraries (DecisionTree.jl, XGBoost.jl) and custom implementations (linear models, KNN, Naive Bayes, ElasticNet, SVM) for the algorithm backends. It reproduces all 7 kernel primitives, all 4 hard constraints, the full strategy layer (screen, tune, stack, compare, validate), and the diagnostics layer (profile, check, drift, enough, leak, calibrate, quick): 22 verbs across 12 algorithm families, with 331 tests. The type DAG is identical: SplitResult, PreparedData, Model, Metrics, and Evidence are distinct named types; the assess-once guard fires on the second call. fit performs per-fold preparation by default.

Parity across three languages required no shared code. Each implementation was built against the grammar specification, not against the other implementations. The verb names change (ml.fit vs ml_fit vs ML.fit). The type structure is frozen. This is the empirical content of the portability claim: a specification precise enough that three separate implementations converge on the same behavior without coordinating their internals.

5.2 The Codd test

Codd ([ref-codd1970relational]) defined the relational model as a mathematical specification (the later “Codd rules” formalized this as a practical conformance standard). SQL implementations could be tested against it: does this database system satisfy the relational algebra? I propose the same spirit for the grammar: does a given implementation satisfy the type DAG and the four hard constraints? The analogy is in spirit (a testable conformance standard), not in substance: Codd’s completeness criterion had an external anchor (first-order predicate calculus expressibility); the seven conditions below are derived from the grammar itself.

Concretely, a conforming implementation must:

  1. 1.

    Produce a Partition from split

  2. 2.

    Require a tagged DataFrame (partition_tag ∈\in {train, valid, dev}) for fit

  3. 3.

    Require a Model for evaluate and assess

  4. 4.

    Reject a second assess call on the same model

  5. 5.

    Perform preparation per fold in declarative mode

  6. 6.

    Make label-based feature selection before split fail at the API boundary (e.g., by rejecting data without split provenance when it enters fit)

  7. 7.

    Return Evidence as a named class that is not implicitly substitutable for Metrics in the host language; isinstance(result, Evidence) must be distinguishable from isinstance(result, Metrics)

The practical value of the Codd test is decidability: without a grammar, “is this workflow methodologically correct?” is a matter of opinion. With it, correctness is enforceable in constant time: seven nodes, four constraints. The test produces a binary verdict, not a judgment call.

Conditions 1–6 and 7 are verifiable from the API surface: fit rejects unregistered data with a PartitionError whose message directs the user to split first. The closed-world limitation of prior versions (where untagged data passed silently) is closed. The Julia implementation serves as a portability test: built from the specification without translating Python or R source code, it satisfies all seven conditions using Julia-native libraries.

5.3 Hierarchy of defaults

The grammar operates at two levels of explicitness:

Declarative (default): ml.fit(s.train, "y") handles algorithm selection, preprocessing, and cross-validation internally. The grammar’s constraints are satisfied automatically. This is the entry point for newcomers and the default mode.

Explicit: Each step can be called independently for full control. ml.prepare(), ml.fit(), ml.evaluate() as separate operations. The grammar’s constraints still apply: assess is still terminal, preparation is still per-fold. But the user sees each intermediate type.

The default mode does the correct thing. The explicit mode makes the types visible.

6 Comparison with Existing Frameworks

6.1 Overview

Production workflow tools (MLflow, ZenML, Kedro, Metaflow) solve execution orchestration and experiment tracking, infrastructure the grammar assumes but does not itself provide. Typed DAG execution frameworks (Flyte, Prefect) enforce input/output type checking between pipeline steps, structurally adjacent to the grammar’s type DAG. Their types serve pipeline wiring correctness, a complementary layer to the grammar’s methodological validity checks. These tools are not compared directly because they operate at the execution layer. The grammar operates at the methodological correctness layer. The two layers compose naturally: a grammar-conforming workflow could run on any of these execution backends.

6.2 tidymodels

Kuhn and Silge ([ref-kuhn2022tidy]) is the closest existing framework. Its recipes enforce per-fold preprocessing when used inside workflows, preventing Class I leakage structurally. It deserves explicit credit as the most important prior work.

The grammar extends tidymodels’ type system one level further. tidymodels types (recipe, parsnip model, workflow) ensure that preprocessing steps are applied consistently, which is the right guarantee at the preprocessing boundary. The grammar adds a guarantee at the assessment boundary: a type that marks a model as terminally assessed, so that repeated test-set evaluation is rejected at call time. The two systems are complementary. The grammar’s terminal assess type is the layer tidymodels does not need to provide because its scope ends before assessment.

6.3 D3M and AutoML grammars

DARPA’s D3M programme (2018–2022) developed a typed primitive taxonomy with ~280 annotated components, input/output type annotations, and automated pipeline search. Drori et al. ([ref-drori2019alphad3m]) extends this with formal context-free grammars over pipeline components.

D3M pioneered the idea that ML workflow components should carry typed annotations, and AlphaD3M showed that a formal grammar over those components could prune the search space effectively. The grammar presented here applies the same typed-primitive principle to a different question. D3M’s types answer “what pipelines can I build?” (which components connect to which). The grammar asks “what workflows are valid?” (which compositions satisfy methodological constraints). The two are complementary: D3M’s component taxonomy could coexist with the grammar’s lifecycle constraints, providing search pruning and correctness checking simultaneously.

6.4 mlr3

Binder et al. ([ref-bischl2021mlr3pipelines]) is the most formally specified existing system. Its PipeOp system defines typed inputs and outputs for each pipeline step using graph-based composition — the strongest prior art for typed ML workflows. mlr3 provides a composition model (how to build pipelines from components). The grammar adds a validity model (which compositions satisfy methodological constraints). The two address different layers, and mlr3’s engineering could serve as an implementation substrate for the grammar’s constraints. The composition algebra is already there. The rejection criterion would be a layer on top.

6.5 The novelty claim

The contribution is the terminal assess constraint: the first type-level enforcement of the evaluate/assess boundary in any ML framework, making repeated test-set assessment rejected at call time in a conforming implementation. The grammar builds on a chain of prior contributions: Kapoor and Narayanan ([ref-kapoor2023leakage]) established the leakage taxonomy across 17 fields; LeakageDetector ([ref-yang2022leakage]) proved that automated detection is feasible; tidymodels solved per-fold preprocessing; D3M and AlphaD3M showed that typed primitives can structure ML pipelines; Sculley et al. ([ref-sculley2015hidden]) named the structural fragility patterns (entanglement, undeclared consumers, correction cascades) that persist even in technically correct pipelines. The grammar adds one layer that this chain had not yet reached: a terminal assess constraint that rejects the two most damaging leakage classes at the API boundary. The companion study ([ref-roth2026landscape]) quantifies why that specific layer matters (dz=0.53d_{z}=0.53–1.111.11).

7 Preliminary Empirical Evidence

My companion study ([ref-roth2026landscape], in preparation) measures leakage effects across 2,047 experimental instances (OpenML ([ref-vanschoren2014openml]) benchmark datasets × 4 algorithms: logistic regression, random forest, decision tree, kk-nearest neighbors). The grammar’s structural claims — which workflows are rejected by type checks or guards — are independent of that evidence and verifiable from the specification in the Appendix alone. The empirical results motivate the constraint design: they explain why Class II and III are targeted and Class I is tolerated despite being structurally addressable.

7.1 Leakage classes by mechanism

Effect sizes are paired Cohen’s dz=d¯/sdd_{z}=\bar{d}/s_{d} (mean of per-dataset leaky-minus-clean AUC differences divided by the standard deviation of those differences). For Class II peeking: dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93 (95% CI [0.86,1.00][0.86,1.00], N=2,047N=2{,}047). Raw AUC inflation (Δ\DeltaAUC) is reported alongside dzd_{z} throughout this paper because dzd_{z} standardizes effect magnitude but obscures absolute scale: a dzd_{z} of 0.93 corresponds to a median AUC inflation of approximately 4.6 hundredths of a point. Whether this magnitude is practically significant depends on the application domain; in high-stakes clinical AI, even small AUC inflation can change treatment decisions. An order-statistics interpretation is also relevant: the peeking experiment selects the best of K=10K=10 model configurations evaluated on the test set. The expected inflation from best-of-KK selection is O⁡(σ​2​ln⁡K)O(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln K}); the grammar’s contribution is making this selection structurally impossible, not discovering that it inflates performance.

The three classes are defined by mechanism (how information crosses the train/test boundary), not by the grammar’s constraints. The classification is grounded in Kaufman et al. ([ref-kaufman2012leakage])’s independent formalization of leakage types and extended with effect-size measurement. The grammar’s constraints were then designed to target the classes with large effects, but the classes exist independently of the grammar.

Class I effects are negligible at any sample size. Class II effects persist across all tested sample sizes (n=50n=50–2,0002{,}000): peeking at test labels inflates performance by dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93 (raw AUC inflation: +0.046+0.046 points). The magnitude decays with nn (the ratio d(50)/d(2000)≈2.1×d(50)/d(2000)\approx 2.1\times for peeking) but does not vanish; the asymptotic floor remains positive. Class III effects are capacity-dependent: decision trees (d=1.11d=1.11) memorize more than random forests (d=0.90d=0.90). The dzd_{z}-values for Class III were measured on LR, RF, DT, and KNN; gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) uses a qualitatively different memorization mechanism (soft memorization via bounded weak learners and shrinkage), and its Class III exposure is untested in this study. The detection floor at N=2,047N=2{,}047 is d=0.057d=0.057 (assuming normality; the heavy-tailed distributions observed in V2, with kurtosis values from 6 to 215, imply that the effective detection floor is somewhat higher). Confidence intervals and full distributional results for all effect sizes are reported in the companion study ([ref-roth2026landscape], in preparation).

7.2 NN-scaling and power law analysis

A follow-up study measured leakage effects across six sample sizes (N∈{50,100,200,500,1000,2000}N\in\{50,100,200,500,1000,2000\}) on 493 OpenML datasets, each with 10 replications per condition. The results confirm and strengthen the mechanistic taxonomy:

All three classes follow d⁡(n)=a⋅n−b+cd(n)=a\cdot n^{-b}+c with R2>0.97R^{2}>0.97. The key result: Class II has a positive asymptotic floor (d∞=0.047d_{\infty}=0.047), while Class III decays toward zero. A nested model comparison between the 3-parameter model (d=a⋅n−b+cd=a\cdot n^{-b}+c) and the 2-parameter alternative (d=a⋅n−bd=a\cdot n^{-b}, i.e., c=0c=0) favors the floor model for Class II (AIC difference >10>10) but not for Class III, where the simpler model fits adequately. This supports the grammar’s unconditional rejection of Class II workflows; the effect does not vanish within the tested range (n=50n=50–2,0002{,}000). Class III’s decay pattern is consistent with a capacity-limited mechanism. The power law is fitted to 6 data points with 3 parameters, leaving 3 residual degrees of freedom; the R2R^{2} values should be interpreted with this caveat. Extrapolation beyond n=2,000n=2{,}000 is not empirically supported.

7.3 Seed cherry-picking scales as log⁡K\log K

Across 1,363 datasets, random forest seed inflation follows inflation=0.00326⋅log⁡(K)+0.00395\text{inflation}=0.00326\cdot\log(K)+0.00395 (R2=0.992R^{2}=0.992), where KK is the number of seeds evaluated. Logistic regression inflation is exactly zero (sd=0.000000\text{sd}=0.000000) because the model is deterministic given the data. The log-scaling has no plateau: extrapolating to K=1000K=1000 yields +0.026+0.026 AUC. This confirms that cherry-picking scales without bound, strengthening the grammar’s assess-once constraint.

7.4 Cross-validation coverage miscalibration

Across 1,903 datasets with 3 algorithms (LR, RF, DT), the nominal 95% confidence interval from kk-fold cross-validation achieves only 55.1% actual coverage (zz-based) or 70.4% (tt-based). This is consistent with Bengio and Grandvalet ([ref-bengio2004noUnbiased]), who proved that no unbiased estimator of CV variance exists. The miscalibration is worst for flexible models (DT: 54.5% zz, 69.3% tt) and best for constrained models (LR: 56.3% zz, 71.9% tt). This implies that evaluate() should report uncertainty with explicit miscalibration warnings rather than nominal confidence intervals.

7.5 Discovery/confirmation replication

All 11 new experiments replicated exactly across independent discovery (k=1,007k=1{,}007) and confirmation (k=1,040k=1{,}040) halves; for example, seed inflation: d=+0.044d=+0.044 vs. d=+0.046d=+0.046. All 17 experiments across both stages replicated. The halves were fixed by MD5 hash of dataset name, applied deterministically before analysis. This is an internal validation procedure (split-half replication), not a formal pre-registration on an external platform. The replication is meaningful; 17/17 effects replicate across independent dataset subsets, and the experiments use only publicly available OpenML datasets, so anyone with sufficient compute can reproduce them. All experiment scripts and raw results will be published alongside the companion study. But this should not be confused with prospective hypothesis registration on OSF or a comparable registry.

7.6 Three predictions from the grammar

The three predictions introduced in Section 3.4 are reported in full here. All were specified in internal design documents before running V2 experiments, though the author had access to V1 results when formulating them. Screen inflation and seed inflation were expected outcomes based on V1 data; the stack prediction was the only genuinely risky hypothesis. Screen inflation is also consistent with the prior literature on selection bias in model evaluation ([ref-cawley2010overfitting]).

  1. 1.

    Screen inflation (d>0d>0): Confirmed: d=+0.27d=+0.27, approximately constant across K∈{1,5,11}K\in\{1,5,11\} (raw: +0.013+0.013, +0.013+0.013, +0.013+0.013 AUC). The KK-invariance implies near-perfect correlation among algorithm performances on these datasets; the inflation reflects the gap between a selected model and a random baseline, not a selection-pressure effect that grows with KK.

  2. 2.

    Stack leakage (d>0d>0): Falsified: d=−0.22d=-0.22. The grammar’s stack() is empirically safe. The meta-learner does not introduce detectable leakage at this scale.

  3. 3.

    Seed inflation (d>0d>0): Confirmed: d=+0.88d=+0.88, prevalence 92%.

Two of three confirmed. One falsified. I predicted that stacking would leak. It did not: d=−0.22d=-0.22 at the tested scale. The grammar’s out-of-fold architecture was sound; my effect-size prediction was not. The data overrode the prediction. The structural claims survive.

7.7 Moderator analysis

Frequentist Spearman correlations between dataset characteristics and leakage severity show weak but statistically significant associations: seed inflation correlates with log nn (r=−0.274r=-0.274, p<0.001p<0.001) and screen inflation with log nn (r=−0.130r=-0.130, p<0.001p<0.001). However, effect sizes are small (r2<0.08r^{2}<0.08), and the practical implication is limited: no dataset characteristic predicts which specific datasets are safe from leakage. The correlations reflect the nn-scaling pattern documented above (larger datasets show smaller absolute effects) rather than a moderator that would exempt certain datasets from the grammar’s constraints. Full moderator analysis, including a planned hierarchical model accounting for dataset clustering, is reported in the companion study ([ref-roth2026landscape], in preparation).

7.8 Implementation stress testing

The three implementations have been tested against 2,805 test cases (1,685 Python, 783 R, 337 Julia) covering edge cases, boundary conditions, and constraint-violation attempts. All three implementations satisfy the 7 Codd test conditions, including condition 7 (Evidence as a named class distinct from Metrics): Python uses Evidence(dict) vs Metrics(dict), R uses ml_evidence vs ml_metrics S3 classes, and Julia uses nominal struct Evidence vs struct Metrics.

8 Discussion

8.1 What the grammar does not do

The grammar prevents structural errors. It does not prevent semantic errors:

This is Chomsky’s crack. “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” is grammatically valid but semantically nonsense ([ref-chomsky1957syntactic]). A workflow that passes all type checks but produces a poor model for semantic reasons is the ML analogue. A diagnostics layer (check, drift, profile, enough) addresses semantic quality as a separate concern.

Structural validity does not imply numerical reproducibility. fit(data, seed=42) and fit(data, seed=43) are grammatically identical; they may produce models with different metrics and different conclusions. Reproducibility requires additional infrastructure beyond fixed seeds (environment versioning, hardware determinism) that the grammar does not formalize. The grammar prevents leakage, not non-reproducibility. Both are correctness concerns; only one is structural.

The primitive set is operation-centric: all seven primitives are verbs. This is a design choice, not an oversight. Validity constraints are enforced at operations, not at values: a DataFrame is neither valid nor invalid in isolation; it becomes invalid when passed to fit without a partition tag. The types (DataFrame, Partition, Model, Metrics) are defined formally in the Appendix and are co-equal in the specification; they appear secondary in the prose because the actionable grammar lives on the verbs, not the values flowing between them.

8.2 Small N

Below approximately N=30N=30, the grammar’s three-way split becomes statistically vacuous. The grammar does not disappear; it contracts:

The deeper constraint is not raw NN but the ratio of events to predictors: logistic regression needs approximately 20 events per predictor ([ref-riley2019minimum]), while tree ensembles need 3,000+ ([ref-vanderploeg2014modern]). The grammar’s real contribution at small NN is discipline: separate what you learn on from what you judge on. That discipline applies at every NN. The mechanism of separation requires a minimum investment of observations.

8.3 Domain scope

The grammar covers tabular binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression, the setting where the companion study’s effect sizes were measured. It does not currently cover deep learning workflows (different type structure: tensors, batches, epochs), unsupervised learning (no target variable, different split semantics), or structured-data modalities where leakage dynamics differ qualitatively: spatial autocorrelation in ecology ([ref-rosenblatt2024data]), tokenization leakage in NLP, linkage disequilibrium in genomics. The grammar also assumes a complete dataset at split time: split takes a full DataFrame and partitions it. Online learning, continual learning, and active learning might violate this foundational assumption: data arrives incrementally, with no complete rectangle to partition. The grammar is scoped to batch supervised learning; its split primitive has no defined semantics for streaming inputs. Both evaluate and assess assume a stationary data-generating process; when the test distribution has shifted since training (concept drift, covariate shift, population change), the grammar’s type guarantees hold but Evidence no longer measures generalization to the current environment. Temporal evaluation primitives are outside this grammar’s Σ\Sigma. The grammar’s constraints and the companion study’s dd-values do not transfer to these domains. The scope is intentional: tabular supervised learning is where the train/test boundary is cleanest and all three leakage classes have been empirically quantified. Extending the grammar to other paradigms requires analogous empirical baselines first.

8.4 External validation

External validation is the missing piece. Whether the grammar reduces leakage errors in classrooms and research pipelines is untested; Wickham had ggplot2 users before the grammar paper, and here the sequence is reversed.

The obvious next test is a randomized between-subjects experiment: participants complete an ML task (e.g., predicting hospital readmission from tabular clinical data) using either sklearn (control) or the grammar’s implementation (treatment). The primary outcome is the leakage rate: the proportion of submitted workflows containing at least one Class II or III violation, scored by an automated checker blind to condition. Secondary outcomes include the magnitude of performance inflation and task completion time. A sample of 40–60 participants (undergraduate or master’s students in a data science course, randomly assigned) would provide adequate power to detect a halving of the leakage rate (from an estimated 30–50% baseline to 15–25%). The experiment requires a certified reference implementation and a scoring rubric defined before data collection. The three implementations described in this paper provide the treatment condition; the study design is left for future work.

8.5 Enforcement gaps

The grammar specifies which workflows are invalid. The implementation enforces this specification imperfectly:

The grammar is a specification; the implementation is an approximation of it. A context-free grammar makes certain strings underivable at the level of the formal system, not at the level of any particular parser; the same distinction applies here. A user who serializes a model and deserializes it (or calls copy.deepcopy(model)) can circumvent the assess-once constraint; a user who mutates a SplitResult’s .test attribute can corrupt the assessment boundary. Both are real gaps.

The partition_tag propagation gap was structurally the most significant in prior versions, and it is an instance of a pattern that recurs whenever a grammar enforces constraints via metadata attributes in a host language whose standard operations do not preserve them. Call this tag erasure: typed metadata set by the grammar is silently discarded by untyped operations in the surrounding environment. In pandas, merge, concat, and groupby strip DataFrame attributes silently; an attribute-based partition_tag is lost after any standard DataFrame manipulation between split and fit.

The current implementation closes this gap via content-addressed partition identity: split computes a deterministic fingerprint of each output partition (SHA-256 over hash_pandas_object values) and registers it in a session-scoped provenance registry that maps fingerprints to partition roles and split lineage. Each verb’s guard queries the registry by content fingerprint rather than reading a metadata attribute. Because the fingerprint is computed from cell values and column names, not from a metadata attribute, it survives DataFrame operations that preserve both row content and column structure (reindexing, dtype coercion). Operations that change content or structure (filtering rows, selecting or adding columns, merging, renaming) produce a new fingerprint that is absent from the registry; the guard rejects the data as unregistered. This is not a loophole; it is the intended behavior: feature engineering between split and fit is outside the grammar’s seven primitives and is rejected at fit’s entry point. The grammar’s answer is prepare inside fit, per fold (Constraint 2). The provenance registry additionally stores split lineage (which split call produced each partition), enabling a cross-verb check at assess time: test data from a different split than the training data is rejected, closing a second-order leakage vector (test-set shopping across splits). Tag erasure is not a bug in any one implementation; it is a structural mismatch between the grammar’s typed requirements and the host environment’s untyped operations. The solution is the architecture the previous paragraph describes: partition provenance stored in a separate structure that host-language operations do not touch by default.

Early SQL implementations violated Codd’s relational model routinely: allowing duplicate rows, failing to enforce referential integrity, permitting NULL semantics that contradicted the specification. The specification remained correct, and implementations improved over decades. The grammar’s enforcement gaps are probably smaller than early SQL’s. The most significant gap, tag erasure, was resolved via content-addressed partition identity in v1.0.0 of the Python implementation. The remaining gaps (runtime circumvention, optimization leakage, stopping criterion) are well understood, and the path to closing them (persistent state, immutable types, affine/linear type system) is established.

Three open flanks define the grammar’s current ceiling. Runtime circumvention: the assess-once guard is enforced at call time, not compile time; it resets on serialization or copy.deepcopy. Optimization leakage: the grammar is a gate, not a schedule; indefinite iteration in the evaluate zone is grammatically valid even when it is methodologically suspect. No stopping criterion: the transition from iteration to commitment is ungoverned. Together, they mark the boundary between structural validity (what the grammar guarantees) and scientific integrity (what a rigorous methodology requires). Structural validity is necessary but not sufficient. A fourth flank, tag erasure, was closed by content-addressed partition identity (described above): partition provenance stored in a registry external to the host language’s metadata system survives the DataFrame operations that previously stripped it.

A fifth gap deserves separate mention: multi-model test-set peeking. The assess-once constraint is per model, not per test set. A practitioner who trains 5 models and assesses each on the same test set has performed model selection on test data, statistically equivalent to evaluating 5 times. The grammar sees 5 independent, valid assessments. A per-dataset constraint (at most one model assessed on any given test set) would close this gap but requires global state across models, breaking the composability that makes the grammar practical. The current design accepts this tradeoff: per-model assess-once catches the most common abuse (re-running the same model after tweaks) while preserving the independence of separate modeling efforts. Users comparing multiple models on the same test set should adjust for multiplicity or use a dedicated comparison protocol; the grammar does not enforce this.

8.6 Production and deployment

A separate objection holds that the grammar governs training-time structure but leaves the deployment lifecycle unaddressed: practitioners may call evaluate() on production batches and treat incoming data as an implicit validation set without the grammar intervening.

The objection assumes a distinction between training-time and production-time that the grammar does not draw. The grammar defines valid workflows as compositions over Σ\Sigma; that definition is not scoped to a single lifecycle. Production monitoring decomposes into the same primitives (drift, split, fit, evaluate, assess) and is therefore a workflow in WW, governed by the same four constraints. If evaluate() on production batches produces leakage, it does so for exactly the same structural reason that evaluate() on a held-out test set does: data has been seen before assess() closes the model. The grammar rejects both on identical grounds. The deployment lifecycle does not require an extension of the grammar; it is another instantiation of it.

8.7 Feature engineering and the closed-world boundary

The grammar’s seven primitives do not include feature engineering: no verb for encoding categoricals, computing lag features, or selecting variables. A natural objection is that the grammar therefore cannot prevent the most common form of preprocessing leakage: computing features on the full dataset before splitting.

The grammar’s answer is that feature engineering belongs inside prepare, which runs inside fit, per fold (Constraint 2). This is not a workaround; it is the structurally correct position. In temporal cross-validation, features derived from the data (rolling averages, lag variables, target encodings) must be computed using only the training data available at each fold’s time cutoff. Computing them before the split uses future data to construct past features, a temporal leakage that inflates performance estimates. The same argument applies to standard cross-validation: target-encoding before the split uses test labels to construct training features. In computationally intensive settings with many features or large datasets, per-fold preparation can become a bottleneck. A future grammar extension may introduce a safe precomputation primitive that runs before split but is restricted to leakage-free transformations (e.g., static type conversions, column selection) while routing target-dependent operations through the per-fold path.

The grammar specifies this position structurally: fit requires data that has passed through split. The implementation enforces this by rejecting data without split provenance: not just data with a known-wrong tag, but any data that has not been registered by split. This forces all feature engineering through prepare per fold: there is no path from raw data to fit that bypasses split.

This closes what appeared to be a closed-world limitation. The grammar does not need to detect pre-split feature engineering; it makes the pre-split path structurally inaccessible. The prepare verb is deliberately opaque, a monolith that handles encoding, scaling, imputation, and derived features internally. Decomposing prepare into typed sub-operations (encode, scale, impute, derive, select) is a natural extension that would make each transformation step visible while preserving the per-fold constraint. That decomposition is left for future work; the current grammar’s guarantee is that prepare runs per fold, and no unregistered data can bypass it.

8.8 Enforcement philosophy

The grammar’s four constraints admit two enforcement strategies. A gate rejects invalid input at every entry point: fit refuses data without split provenance, making the unsplit path fail at entry. A funnel makes the correct path the path of least resistance without blocking the incorrect one. The distinction matters because Class II and III protection is downstream of split: a user who never splits gets no partition tags, and the guards at evaluate and assess never fire. Advisory protection that only catches mistakes by users who already do the right thing is circular.

The implementation therefore enforces split provenance structurally: fit, evaluate, assess, and validate all reject data that has not passed through split. Every guard checks the content-addressed registry; data with no fingerprint match (unregistered) is rejected with a message directing the user to split first. This closes the dependency: the guards that prevent Class II and III leakage (dz=0.53d_{z}=0.53–1.111.11) are activated by the same mechanism that prevents Class I (|d|<0.1|d|<0.1). The cost is real: the simple path (ml.fit(df, "y") without a prior split call) no longer works by default. A configuration switch (config(guards="off")) disables all guards for exploration, education, and rapid prototyping where structural enforcement is unnecessary. This is an explicit exit from the grammar’s jurisdiction, analogous to Rust’s unsafe blocks, which do not weaken the type system but mark where the programmer has left it.

The three implementations enforce provenance through different mechanisms: Python uses content-addressed fingerprinting (SHA-256 over cell values, session-scoped registry), R uses DataFrame attributes (attr(data, "_ml_partition")), and Julia uses DataFrames.metadata(). The mechanisms currently differ in robustness to host-language operations (fingerprinting survives copy() and reindexing; attributes and metadata are lost on reconstruction). The R and Julia implementations are expected to converge on content-addressed fingerprinting before release. The grammatical semantics are already identical across all three: every verb rejects data without split provenance when guards are active. The grammar is language-agnostic; the enforcement adapts to each host’s idioms.

8.9 Implementation variance

Two conforming implementations of the same algorithm can produce different predictive surfaces. In cross-engine experiments, implementations of SVM using different solvers produced R2R^{2} values of 0.964 and 0.917 on identical data with identical hyperparameters. The grammar guarantees type-correctness; it does not guarantee behavioral equivalence across engines. This is a genuine expressiveness limitation that has to be acknowledged.

8.10 Data flow and operational flow

The type DAG models data flow: which types are produced and consumed by each primitive. Strategy verbs (tune, screen, stack) have implicit operational semantics that the type DAG does not capture. tune calls fit and evaluate internally; its type signature tune :: Model × HyperparameterSpace → TuningResult hides this orchestration. The grammar specifies what types flow between operations but not which operations trigger which. For correctness checking this is sufficient: the type guard at each primitive boundary is what prevents leakage, not the order in which strategies invoke primitives internally.

The composition graph reveals that the seven primitives are not structural peers. evaluate is a hub: six verbs compose through it internally (assess, validate, compare, screen, shelf, and tune all call evaluate on their data). This hub structure has a practical consequence for guard design: evaluate carries the tightest partition constraint (rejecting test-tagged data), yet every finalization verb must route test data through it. The implementation resolves this via a trusted/untrusted calling context — public calls enforce the guard; internal composition bypasses it. But the type DAG does not represent this distinction. A complete account of ML workflow structure would distinguish the data flow graph from the control flow graph; the current grammar covers the former.

The control-flow gap is most visible in the strategy verbs’ implicit temporal shapes: tune is iterative (a loop that fits and evaluates repeatedly until convergence), screen is parallel (multiple algorithms evaluated simultaneously against the same Partition), and stack is sequential-then-meta (base models trained independently in the first pass, then a meta-learner trained on their out-of-fold predictions in the second). These temporal shapes are nowhere in the type signatures; they emerge from the strategy definitions, not from the type DAG. A practitioner reading only the type DAG cannot infer that tune is a loop and screen is a fan-out. The grammar covers data flow; a complete account would also formalize control flow. That extension is left for future work.

8.11 Structural severity and optimization leakage

The grammar is a gate, not a schedule: it controls which data flows to which primitive but does not govern how many times the iterate zone runs or when the transition to assess is triggered.

The grammar enforces structural severity: assess uses held-out data that has not participated in any prior training or evaluation call. This closes data leakage. It does not close optimization leakage: a practitioner who runs screen() with 11 algorithms, tune() with 500 hyperparameter configurations, and then calls assess() has made hundreds of model selection decisions on the validation set. The grammar considers this valid. Statistically, the final assess result is biased upward because the model was selected to look good on validation data. The grammar prevents test-set leakage but does not prevent validation-set overfitting through repeated evaluation. This is the dominant failure mode in modern ML practice and the grammar’s most significant limitation.

Mayo ([ref-mayo1996]) requires that a hypothesis passes a severe test only if it would probably have failed the test were it false. The grammar satisfies the structural condition: the assessor is held-out data independent of training. It does not enforce the epistemic condition: the model could have been tuned until evaluation looked good, in which case a weak model may still pass assess on a favorable split. The evaluation metric was optimized rather than simply measured, a familiar pattern in model selection that the grammar does not currently address.

Nested cross-validation partially addresses this: the outer loop provides an unbiased estimate of generalization performance while the inner loop handles model selection. The grammar is compatible with nested CV — it is a valid workflow within the grammar’s scope; it does not require it. For high-stakes applications, nested CV or a pre-registered stopping criterion (how many evaluation iterations are permitted, or what convergence condition triggers assess) would close the optimization leakage gap. The grammar specifies the type boundary; it does not specify the transition condition. That specification is left to the practitioner.

A typed gate state — a permission sort that transitions GateState ∈\in {Locked, Unlocked} when assess is first called — would make the temporal boundary explicit in the type system but would not close this gap. A gate records when access was granted, not whether access was earned. The distinction matters: a model that passed only because the practitioner iterated evaluation until metrics looked favorable would still unlock the gate. Closing both gaps simultaneously requires a more expressive type: a gate that cannot open unless a pre-registered stopping criterion has been satisfied. That system — typed permission conditioned on pre-registered termination — is the minimal extension that would enforce both structural severity and epistemic legitimacy jointly. The current grammar enforces one; achieving the other is left to pre-registration protocol, not type enforcement.

9 Conclusion

The grammar of ML workflows shifts where the work happens. The evaluate/assess boundary is not a rule to follow; it is a constraint the implementation enforces. The types remember so you don’t have to.

Seven primitives, four constraints, three separate implementations, 2,805 tests, and a companion study across 2,047 experimental instances supplemented by 3,759 nn-scaling, seed-stability, and coverage instances ([ref-roth2026landscape]): the grammar holds. The leakage classes it rejects produce large standardized effects (dz=0.93d_{z}=0.93–1.111.11; raw AUC inflation +0.02+0.02–0.090.09 points) that persist across all tested sample sizes (n=50n=50–2,0002{,}000) with a positive asymptotic floor; the class it tolerates does not (|d|<0.1|d|<0.1). Three testable predictions: two confirmed, one falsified. The grammar is falsifiable and survives the test.

The type DAG and four constraints are frozen: they define what a conforming implementation must satisfy. The verb names, function signatures, and language binding are the changeable surface. The Julia implementation — built from the specification without translating Python or R source, reproducing all 7 primitives, 4 constraints, and 22 verbs across 12 algorithm families — demonstrates that the specification is sufficient for independent reimplementation. The open empirical question is whether the grammar reduces leakage errors in practice. The test is straightforward: a randomized study comparing leakage rates in student or researcher code written with the grammar versus without it. That test would require a reference implementation whose conformance to the type DAG and seven Codd conditions is certified, so that “written with the grammar” means the same thing across conditions. Three certified implementations now exist. The grammar makes the hypothesis precise enough to run that test.

Appendix: Formal Specification

9.1 Type system

The grammar is a typed specification over eight types. Each primitive has a type signature, a guard (precondition checked at call time), and an effect (state mutation after call). Two types are terminal (their values feed no further primitive):

† Predictions is not terminal in stacking strategies: the stack strategy reshapes out-of-fold predictions into a new DataFrame and passes it to a second fit call (the meta-learner). In the grammar’s 7-primitive linear DAG, no primitive accepts Predictions directly as a typed input; the reshape is performed by the strategy orchestration, not a primitive.

Two embedded types appear in the sort table above but are not primitive sorts:

  • •

    DataFrame_numeric: a DataFrame where every column is numeric; a structural subtype of DataFrame (all rows of DataFrame_numeric are valid DataFrame values but not vice versa). Produced by prepare; consumed by model algorithms.

  • •

    Transformer: an interface type satisfying state.transform(X: DataFrame) → DataFrame_numeric. It encodes the fit-time preprocessing state so that validation data can be transformed consistently without re-fitting. Not a free-standing sort; it is a field type embedded in PreparedData.

  • •

    partition_tag: an enum attribute {None, train, valid, test, dev} on every DataFrame. Not a separate sort; it is an attribute of the DataFrame sort. Freshly loaded data carries None; split assigns train, valid, test; accessing s.dev (train ∪\cup valid) assigns dev.

9.2 Primitive operations

Each primitive σ\sigma has a type signature, a guard G⁡(σ)G(\sigma) (precondition checked at call time), and an effect E⁡(σ)E(\sigma) (state mutation after call):

9.3 When is a workflow valid?

A workflow (a sequence of primitive calls) is valid if:

  1. 1.

    Types connect: each primitive’s output type matches the next primitive’s expected input type.

  2. 2.

    Guards pass: each primitive’s precondition holds at call time, given all prior effects.

  3. 3.

    Effects apply in order: state mutations (e.g., model.assessed ← true) accumulate sequentially.

A workflow is invalid if any step fails a type check or a guard. The four hard constraints are guards in this sense: not rules a user must remember, but checks that reject invalid workflows at call time.

Note on evaluate guard. The guard on evaluate rejects test-tagged data; it accepts train and valid partitions. Evaluating on training data is legitimate (train-vs-valid score comparison for overfitting diagnosis). The guard prevents test data from entering the iterate cycle: if evaluate accepted test data, the practitioner could iterate on test-set feedback, which is structurally equivalent to training on the test set. The assess primitive is the only path for test data. This is a design decision: evaluate is the practice exam (repeatable, on validation data); assess is the final exam (terminal, on test data).

Note on branching strategies. This definition covers linear workflows. Branching strategies (screen, tune, stack) involve parallel or iterated applications of the same primitives; their validity follows from applying the same type signatures and guards to each branch independently.

Note on domain specializations. split admits domain specializations (split_temporal, split_group) that share its type signature but carry additional guards specific to a scientific domain. This is a representational mechanism, not a primitive extension: the guard set G⁡(split)G(\text{split}) is parameterized by domain, but the type signature and position in the DAG are invariant. A grammar for time series forecasting inherits all 7 primitives and adds temporal guards to split; the kernel is unchanged.

Scope. The guarantees apply to programs that compose the grammar’s 7 primitives. Operations outside these seven (arbitrary DataFrame transformations, external feature selection, direct attribute mutation) are outside the grammar’s scope. The grammar enforces its own API boundary; it cannot enforce what happens in surrounding code.
